```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

`shiny::testServer()` works with async reactives as it does with plain ones,
with one difference: a task runs in a worker, so its result is not there the
moment you set an input. The test has to let the worker finish and let Shiny
see the result. This vignette shows the few lines that do that, using only
the mock session's public methods.

```{r setup}
library(shiny)
library(shinyasync)
library(testthat)
```

## Daemons

Start a small pool at the top of each test and shut it down when the test
ends. Tests then run the same whether or not the app under test calls
`pool_async()`, and never depend on a pool left behind by another test.

```{r pool}
local_pool <- function(n = 2, env = parent.frame()) {
  mirai::daemons(n, dispatcher = TRUE)
  withr::defer(mirai::daemons(0), envir = env)
}
```

If a test does not start daemons, the first task starts the default pool with
a message, held by the mock session, which is also fine for a one-off test.

## Waiting for a result

Two things must happen before a test can read a result. `later::run_now()`
runs the event loop, which delivers the worker's result to the session.
`session$flushReact()` then re-runs the reactives that depend on it, as the
real session would. Repeat both until the condition you care about holds:

```{r wait-for}
wait_for <- function(cond, session, timeout = 15) {
  start <- Sys.time()
  repeat {
    session$flushReact()
    if (isTRUE(shiny::isolate(cond()))) {
      # Let observers see a value that arrived during the last flush.
      session$flushReact()
      return(invisible(TRUE))
    }
    if (difftime(Sys.time(), start, units = "secs") > timeout) {
      stop(
        "Timed out after ", timeout, "s waiting for: ",
        paste(deparse(body(cond)), collapse = " "),
        call. = FALSE
      )
    }
    later::run_now(0.05)
  }
}
```

The second flush after the condition holds lets an observer that depends on
the value run before the test goes on to check what it did.

The condition is any reactive read: the value, `status_async()` or
`has_value_async()`. The read runs inside `isolate()`, so it does not register
dependencies, but it still starts a task that has not run yet, the same way an
output reading the reactive would.

Reading a value that is not there yet halts, as `req()` does, and a halt
inside `expect_equal()` is a confusing failure. `peek()` reads a reactive
and returns a marker instead:

```{r peek}
peek <- function(r) {
  tryCatch(shiny::isolate(r()), shiny.silent.error = function(e) "<halted>")
}
```

Put the three helpers in `tests/testthat/helper-async.R` and every test file
sees them.

## A first test

The server below fits a model in a worker. Set an input, wait for the status to
settle, then read the value exactly as you would in a plain Shiny test.

```{r first-test}
server <- function(input, output, session) {
  fit <- reactiveAsync({
    lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars[seq_len(input$rows), ])
  })
  output$slope <- renderText(round(coef(fit())[["wt"]], 2))
}

test_that("the slope updates when the rows change", {
  local_pool()
  testServer(server, {
    session$setInputs(rows = 32)
    wait_for(function() status_async(fit) == "success", session)
    expect_equal(output$slope, "-5.34")

    session$setInputs(rows = 10)
    wait_for(function() output$slope != "-5.34", session)
    expect_equal(status_async(fit), "success")
  })
})
```

Reading `fit()` before the first result arrives halts silently, as `req()`
does, so the test waits for the status rather than the value. After the first
result, reading the value during a refresh returns the previous one; the second
wait above uses the output changing as its condition for that reason.

## Status, buttons and cancellation

Statuses follow the task. A `bindEvent()` task is `"idle"` until its event,
`"running"` while the worker has it, and `"success"` or `"error"` after.
`cancel_async()` returns it to `"idle"` while keeping the last value.

```{r button}
server <- function(input, output, session) {
  sim <- reactiveAsync({
    Sys.sleep(2)
    mean(rnorm(input$n))
  }) |> bindEvent(input$go)
  observe(cancel_async(sim)) |> bindEvent(input$stop)
}

test_that("a button task runs on click and stops on cancel", {
  local_pool()
  testServer(server, {
    session$setInputs(n = 100)
    expect_equal(status_async(sim), "idle")

    session$setInputs(go = 1)
    expect_equal(status_async(sim), "running")

    session$setInputs(stop = 1)
    expect_equal(status_async(sim), "idle")
    expect_false(has_value_async(sim))
  })
})
```

`session$setInputs()` flushes the session, so the status is `"running"` as
soon as the click is set. That only holds because the task has work to do:
a task that finishes within the flush that dispatched it settles in that
flush, and a test that reads its status straight after `setInputs()` sees
`"success"`. The cancelled run had not produced a result, so there is no
previous value to keep and `has_value_async()` is `FALSE`.

## Errors

A failure in the worker surfaces when the reactive is read, as it would from
`reactive()`. Wait for the status to become `"error"`, then expect the error
on the read.

```{r errors}
server <- function(input, output, session) {
  parsed <- reactiveAsync(jsonlite::fromJSON(input$text))
}

test_that("a worker error is re-thrown on read", {
  local_pool()
  testServer(server, {
    session$setInputs(text = "{not json")
    wait_for(function() status_async(parsed) == "error", session)
    expect_error(parsed(), "lexical error")
  })
})
```

## Side effects

`observeAsync()` has no value to read. Its handle reports the status, and the
side effect is what the test checks: here a line written to a log file.

```{r observe}
log_path <- tempfile(fileext = ".log")

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  logged <- observeAsync(cat(input$spot, file = log_path, sep = "\n", append = TRUE))
}

test_that("each selected spot is logged", {
  local_pool()
  testServer(server, {
    session$setInputs(spot = "Muizenberg")
    wait_for(function() logged$status() == "success", session)
    expect_equal(readLines(log_path), "Muizenberg")
  })
})
```

The observer starts on the next flush, like `observe()`, so there is nothing
to read first. `status_async(logged)` reads the same status as `logged$status()`.

## Values fed by hand

`reactiveValAsync()` is set from an observer, usually with a mirai started
by `mirai_async()`. Test it as any `reactiveVal()`, waiting for the task
the setter was handed:

```{r reactiveval}
rank_spots <- function(spots) sort(spots)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  ranking <- reactiveValAsync()
  observe(ranking(mirai_async(rank_spots(input$spots)))) |> bindEvent(input$rank)
}

test_that("the ranking arrives after the click", {
  local_pool()
  testServer(server, {
    session$setInputs(spots = c("Kommetjie", "Muizenberg", "Elands Bay"))
    expect_null(ranking())

    session$setInputs(rank = 1)
    wait_for(function() has_value_async(ranking), session)
    expect_equal(ranking()[[1]], "Elands Bay")
  })
})
```

Before the click the value is `NULL`, as it would be for a `reactiveVal()`
created without one; only `reactiveAsync()` halts until its first result.
`mirai_async()` ships `rank_spots()` with the task, as it would
a helper from the app's `R/` directory.

## Queued runs

With `mode = "queue"` every change runs, in order, where the default would
cancel the superseded ones. An observer collecting the results into a
`reactiveVal()` is the easiest way to see the order:

```{r queue}
save_favourite <- function(spot) paste("saved", spot)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  saved <- reactiveAsync({
    Sys.sleep(0.2)
    save_favourite(input$favourite)
  }, mode = "queue")
  seen <- reactiveVal(character())
  observe(seen(c(isolate(seen()), saved())))
}

test_that("every favourite is saved, in order", {
  local_pool()
  testServer(server, {
    session$setInputs(favourite = "Kommetjie")
    session$setInputs(favourite = "Muizenberg")
    session$setInputs(favourite = "Elands Bay")
    wait_for(function() identical(peek(saved), "saved Elands Bay"), session)
    expect_equal(seen(), c("saved Kommetjie", "saved Muizenberg", "saved Elands Bay"))
  })
})
```

The three inputs are set before the first task finishes. A queued reactive
starts, like any `reactiveAsync()`, only once something reads it, which the
observer does on the first flush.

## Chained reactives

An async reactive that reads another one keeps its previous value and reports
`"running"` while its upstream is catching up, then runs once on the settled
value. A test can see each step:

```{r chain}
server <- function(input, output, session) {
  fit <- reactiveAsync({
    Sys.sleep(1)
    lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars[seq_len(input$rows), ])
  })
  predicted <- reactiveAsync(predict(fit(), data.frame(wt = 3)))
}

test_that("a prediction waits for the model it depends on", {
  local_pool()
  testServer(server, {
    session$setInputs(rows = 32)
    wait_for(function() has_value_async(predicted), session)
    first <- predicted()

    session$setInputs(rows = 10)
    expect_equal(status_async(predicted), "running")
    expect_equal(peek(predicted), first)
    wait_for(function() !identical(peek(predicted), first), session)
    expect_equal(status_async(fit), "success")
  })
})
```

Waiting on the downstream reactive is enough: reading `predicted` starts
`fit`, and the second wait ends only when a new model has been fitted and
predicted from.

## Modules

Nothing changes for a module: pass the module server to `testServer()` and the
same helpers apply to the reactives it defines or returns.

```{r modules}
summaryServer <- function(id) {
  moduleServer(id, function(input, output, session) {
    s <- reactiveAsync(summary(mtcars[[input$column]]))
    output$text <- renderPrint(s())
    s
  })
}

test_that("the module summarises the chosen column", {
  local_pool()
  testServer(summaryServer, {
    session$setInputs(column = "mpg")
    wait_for(function() has_value_async(s), session)
    expect_equal(s()[["Max."]], 33.9)
  })
})
```
